text: USF Biomed Sciences freshman (international, H-4 visa). Transfer to UF for Finance or Mechanical Engineering? — Why I'm reconsidering: - I'm not a US citizen. I'm on an H-4 dependent visa and will likely have to switch to F-1 at 21, which makes me an international applicant for med school. - From what I've researched, only a small fraction of US med schools accept international students, and many of those require extra financial guarantees. I estimate my chances at roughly 1 in 4. - If med school doesn't work out, a Biomedical Sciences degree on its own doesn't lead to many jobs, and as an international student I need a degree that gets me hired and sponsored. - I also got into UF originally and still want to be there. Option 1: Finance at UF (Warrington) - Pros: strong recruiting network at UF, the prerequisites are realistic for me (business math, econ, accounting), and I'd likely have a high GPA. - Cons: finance isn't STEM-designated, so I'd only get 12 months of OPT (work authorization after graduation) instead of 36. That means one shot at the H-1B lottery. It's also very GPA-competitive for transfers, and I'd arrive as a junior, partway into internship recruiting. Option 2: Mechanical Engineering at UF - Pros: STEM degree, so 36 months of OPT and three H-1B lottery chances. Engineers are in steady demand and get sponsored more often. - Cons: the transfer prerequisites are much heavier: Calc 1–3, Differential Equations, calculus-based Physics 1–2, and Chem. My math and physics background is weaker than my friends' who are in engineering, and I'd have to fit all of that in before transferring, likely pushing my timeline back. TL;DR: International (H-4) USF Biomed freshman with roughly a 1 in 4 shot at med school. text: stem opt extension NOIR (notice of intent to revoke) — my stem-opt extension got approved on 8/31 after responding to the RFE, and then i received an email on 9/1 regarding the NOIR. i did a MBA in both data analytics (52.1301) and general management (52.0201). the noir states the following. does anyone have any advice to go about this? "A review of your application and supporting documents submitted, as well as the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), indicates that you submitted a concentration to qualify for STEM. However, a student’s completion of a concentration, specialization, minor, or certificate cannot be used to qualify for STEM OPT. Per 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)(2)(iii), “the degree that is the basis for the application for the OPT extension must be contained within a category on the \[DHS\] STEM Designated Degree Program List.” Any ancillary concentrations, specializations, minors, or certificates earned with the degree cannot be considered as part of the STEM degree when the degree itself is not a STEM designated degree. DHS provides further clarification in the Federal Register Notice. According to the Update to the Department of Homeland Security STEM Designated Degree Program List, 89 FR 59748 (July 23, 2024), only qualifying majors may meet the requirements for STEM extensions: “In 2016, DHS published a final rule providing a 24-month extension of OPT for F-1 nonimmigrant students who majored in a designated STEM field of study. See 81 FR 13040 (Mar. 11, 2016).” To qualify for the STEM OPT extension, the degree that is the basis for the extension must be a bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral degree that is assigned a Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP) code that appears on the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List. A concentration, though it may have an assigned STEM CIP code, cannot be used to qualify for a STEM extension. The acceptable STEM CIP code must be assigned to the student’s major. According to your Request for Evidence response, received on August 27, 2026, STEM CIP code 52.1301, Management Science, is for one of your concentrations. As your SEVIS record indicates that you are using a concentration, and the concentration is not eligible for STEM OPT, you are ineligible for employment authorization under 8 CFR § 274a.12(c)(3)(i)(C). Please provide evidence of your attainment of a bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral degree with a STEM major and corresponding STEM CIP code that appears on the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List and Form I-20 reflecting necessary DSO updates to your SEVIS record.

text: OPT Premium Processing Delay Fix (w/ evidence) — There have been some very useful threads on how to fix delayed OPT PP once it falls outside the guaranteed 30-business-day window, like this one (OPT Premium Processing Delay Fix : r/f1visa [link]). This post is more about substantiating some already-proposed ideas with direct evidence. Hopefully it will help anyone who suffers from the same pain prioritize their strategies when trying to get their OPT approved. To illustrate the priority, I briefly summarize my action timeline alongside my processing timeline here (all events happened in 2026): * 6/18: Submitted Form I-765 with premium processing. * 7/7: Completed bio, premium processing clock restarted. * 8/18: Passed 30-business-day window. * 8/20: Called the number 866-315-5718 on premium processing receipt. Spoke to an agent by saying the word "request infopass", but was told they can do nothing other than wait. * 8/21: Reached out to a senator and requested that they file a congressional inquiry. * 8/24: The senator's aide replied that they filed the inquiry and will keep me posted. * 8/26: Email [PSC-premium.processing@uscis.dhs.gov](mailto:PSC-premium.processing@uscis.dhs.gov) and ask them to review the case. * 8/27: Called 866-315-5718 again and asked to speak to a tier-2 agent. Was told the call would be scheduled within 30 days. Tried to flag it as an emergency but didn't succeed. * 8/28: Contacted another senator and was told they would reach out soon. Contacted the International Office and asked them to submit an SEVP inquiry. * 8/31 - 9/3: Emailed [PSC-premium.processing@uscis.dhs.gov](mailto:PSC-premium.processing@uscis.dhs.gov) daily to request that the case be moved to the adjudication team. * 9/3: Received a reply to the email sent on 9/2 stating the case needs additional review, with no timeline provided. * 9/4: API showed an update was made, but no action code. * 9/5: Received approval email. Based on the timeline provided above, we can see the most important thing is *EMAIL PP TEAM MULTIPLE TIMES*. Even though many have said not to email the PP team every day, as it may jeopardize your case. However, in my experience, a single email can get buried and never get a reply: my emails sent on 8/26, 8/31, and 9/1 never got a response, and they only replied to my email sent on 9/2. This proves they are NOT responding to emails in the order they were sent, which means no matter how long you wait, a cold email remains cold. Another thing to note: From my conversation with the agents on the calls, they've apparently permanently closed the PP number 866-315-5718. They always reroute the call to the team that handles OPT without PP. Therefore, even a tier-2 officer will not have much more information, as PP falls outside their normal scope of work. The evidence is as follows: 1. In 2 calls, I was told that USCIS runs two separate expedition systems: one only accepts requests where the case has exceeded the general OPT timeline (180 days); the other one is PP. Once a case enters PP, no further expedition can be done because PP itself is a way of expedition, and there is no "expedition of an expedition". 2. I asked to schedule a callback from a tier-2 officer within 3 days, saying I would lose my job offer, but they rejected it every time. Their reason is exactly Point 1, and they further say that since PP is outside their scope, any tier-2 officer will have no different information than they do. Overall, I think it's frustrating that they've closed the PP hotline and only reply by email. But it is what it is, and we have to adapt. Best luck to anyone who is still waiting, and hope everyone gets approved timely!

text: Fragomen writes to ICE/SEVP urging revision of recent CPT guidance for International Students — Pt 3 seems to suggest the recent interpretation in the circular is incorrect 3. The Regulation Does Not Mandate a Practical Training Requirement for Every Student Pursuing the Same Degree The regulation allows CPT when practical training is integral to an established curriculum; it does not require every student in the broader degree program to complete the training. The regulation lists “alternative work/study, internship, cooperative education or any other type of required internship or practicum.” The word “or” separates distinct forms of training, while “required” appears only in the final category. By treating “required” as if it modified every listed form of training, the Broadcast Messages impose an additional condition that does not appear in the regulation. SEVP’s interpretation also overlooks how academic programs operate in practice. A school may offer an elective course, concentration, or pathway in which practical training is required for participating students even though other students complete the degree through a different route. A school may need flexibility when placements are unavailable or when required to offer an alternative to accommodate a student disability. SEVP should therefore evaluate whether practical training is genuinely integrated into the student’s curriculum, not whether every student pursuing the same degree must complete it.

text: Can you still do a second masters degree as a PhD student under the new rule? — My understanding is that you probably won't be able to. But I could be wrong and would like to hear alternative interpretations. In fact, I just completed my second masters degree as a PhD student. And here's my understanding based on my experience. Let's say you're a PhD student in mathematics and want to pick up a second masters degree in statistics to fatten up your CV without losing track of your PhD. That's not a bad idea at all. Many people have done it before. Here's the tricky part though. Most degree programs have minimum residency requirements. That means in this scenario, you'll have to change your I-20 to the statistics program, maintain that status for at least one semester (or a year depending on the program's residency requirement), and then transfer back to the PhD program in maths with an updated I-20. Now, the thing is, under the new rule, you can't drop down to lower degree levels and change your I-20 as you see fit any more. That means even though it's technically not against the rule to pick up an incidental masters during your PhD, it's hard to fulfill the minimum residency requirement. There are probably masters programs out there without residency requirements. There are perhaps en-route masters degrees integrated into your PhD curriculum that do not require I-20 updates. I don't know. Those exceptions probably exist. But it's definitely more difficult for PhD students to pursue multiple degrees in the future. After all, how many masters programs would allow you to maintain your primary educational objective (PhD) without enrolling in their programs on I-20? Not a lot I guess. That's the real problem. So my answer is: almost impossible with a small number of exceptions, even though it's technically not banned on paper.

text: My opt got denied — August 14, 2025, my OPT was denied. I had a job lined up to start on October 1st and so many dreams for my future. Because the denial came after my grace period had already ended, my only option was to file an I-290B Motion to Reopen/Reconsider. They made me wait 6 months in absolute limbo, only to deny the I-290B as well. I was forced to pack up my entire life and return to my home country. It has now been 7 months since I came back, and I am still stuck without a proper job. Watching everything I worked for collapse because of immigration bureaucracy has broken me mentally. As a Christian, this has also triggered a massive crisis of faith. I feel angry at God, deeply hurt, and completely lost. At the same time, I catch myself feeling guilty—wondering if I am just a sinner being punished, or what I could have possibly done wrong to deserve this. People tell me to just "have faith," but I feel hollow and exhausted. I feel isolated, stuck, and overwhelmed by how unfair it all feels. Iam posting here to ask: For those who lost their OPT/I-290B and had to leave: How did you cope with the grief of losing your U.S. plans, and what concrete steps helped you rebuild your career back home? * For fellow believers: Has anyone else gone through a complete collapse of their life plans and wrestled with this level of anger and guilt toward God? How do you keep going when faith feels empty? UPDATE / EDIT: Thank you to everyone who read, upvoted, and took the time to leave a comment. I never expected this post to reach over 42k views and 43 comments. I am not a bot—just someone sitting here in shock, trying to process how many people read my story. I am going to take my time to read through all of your responses carefully, and I will reply as I can. To answer those asking about the reason for denial: it was due to a filing timeline error with the OPT I-20. I requested my I-20 early wanting to be prepared, but ended up filing the I-765 a few days past the 30-day requirement window from when the DSO issued it. I played strictly by the rules—I never worked off-campus, stayed fully compliant, and chose not to file for asylum because I didn't want to take a path that wasn't genuine or legal for my situation. I survived off the savings I built up while working on-campus, trying to handle everything honorably. That is why this hurts so deeply and feels so completely devastating. I feel I didn't deserve this from God. I can't believe this happened—He promised me so much, and now everything is gone. I have no one here to guide me. Even getting to the U.S., doing on-campus work, and securing that job—I did everything on my own by following what I believed He called me to do. Then in just a few moments, it all went away. Now I have no plan, no guidance, and I honestly don't even know how to apply to jobs or navigate immigration systems in other countries. At 25, having lived a life focused on doing the right thing, staying out of trouble, avoiding drinking or relationships while waiting for marriage, and striving to honor God, I feel crushed and lost. Having everything in place, only to watch it collapse over a paperwork deadline, leaves me feeling deeply hurt, angry, and completely uncertain about what comes next. I truly appreciate those who shared practical advice, spiritual perspectives, and support. I am taking this one day at a time while I read through your thoughts.
